standard.title: Evaluate texts using metalanguage
standard.description: reflect on and evaluate target language texts, using metalanguage to discuss language structures and features
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare target language structures with English using familiar metalanguage (AC9LS8EU03). They have not yet reflected on and evaluated target language texts analytically — moving from identifying features to explaining how language choices create effect, register and meaning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — analysing how grammatical, vocabulary and textual choices create effect, establish register and convey meaning across different text types and purposes.

nodes.label: Analysing textual coherence and structure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the structural and cohesive features of a target language text that contribute to its coherence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text and explain how they contribute to the text's coherence or purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how introductions, summaries, cohesive devices and paragraph structure contribute to text-level coherence; compare structural conventions across text types; use metalanguage to discuss textual organisation.
wider: Compare the structural conventions of equivalent text types across the target language and English — identify where organisation reflects different cultural or rhetorical expectations
Reconstruct or repair a structurally incomplete or incoherent target language text — explain the structural choices made

response_modes.reason: Textual analysis requires students to move from what a text says to how it is organised to achieve its purpose. Explicit analysis frameworks (purpose → audience → structure → cohesion) support this move before independent analysis is possible.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text using metalanguage
Explains how each identified feature contributes to the text's coherence or purpose

nodes.label: Analysing how language choices create register and effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how grammatical and vocabulary choices in a target language text establish register, shade meaning and create specific effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language choices (vocabulary or grammar) in a target language text and explain how each contributes to register or effect.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how formal and informal registers are constructed through language choices; explain how tense, modality, vocabulary and syntax shade meaning and create tone; use metalanguage to discuss and compare language choices across texts.
wider: Compare how the same content is expressed in formal and informal target language registers — identify the specific language features that signal each register
Investigate how social media, technology or globalisation has influenced target language choices — identify specific examples of language change and discuss their implications
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysing how language choices create register and effect is the core analytical move of EU03. Without it, students can label grammatical features but cannot explain why they matter — the 'reflect and evaluate' demand of the descriptor is not met. This also underpins EC06's purposeful text creation at Y9-10.

response_modes.reason: The move from describing a language feature to explaining its effect requires explicit analytical scaffolding — 'this word is X, which creates Y effect because Z'. Modelled analysis and discussion-based evaluation of choices build this metalinguistic reasoning.

Language choice analysis must be practised across varied text types and registers to be generalisable — register analysis developed only through formal texts will not transfer to digital or informal contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Metalinguistic analysis of how language choices create effect is a transferable analytical skill that extends beyond the target language. Students who develop this capacity have qualitatively better engagement with all texts — in any language.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific language choices in a target language text and explains their contribution to register or effect
Uses metalanguage accurately to discuss language features rather than only describing them in general terms

nodes.label: Evaluating and comparing texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate and compare target language texts, using metalanguage to analyse how language structures and features serve different purposes and audiences.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two target language texts using metalanguage — identify at least two differences in language choices and explain how each reflects the different purpose or audience.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate and compare texts across text types, registers and purposes; discuss how language change (globalisation, technology, social media) affects target language usage; use metalanguage to conduct and present comparative text analyses.
wider: Research the influence of other languages or cultural contact on target language vocabulary over time — identify specific examples and discuss the mechanisms of language change
Produce a text that deliberately imitates the register and conventions of a target language text type — explain the choices made with reference to the model

response_modes.reason: Evaluating and comparing texts integrates structural analysis (node 1) and register/effect analysis (node 2) into a full metalinguistic response. The teaching investment is in tasks that require genuine comparison rather than parallel descriptions of two separate texts.

success_criteria: Compares at least two target language texts using metalanguage, identifying differences in language choices
Explains how identified differences reflect the different purposes or audiences of the texts — not only describes the features
